Energy Demand Analysis and Forecasting¶

Author: Adam Lawit¶

Objective: Create and evaluate multiple forecasting approaches to predict electrical demand over an adjustable period using hourly CAISO data.¶

The goal is to:

  • Capture daily seasonality (24-hour cycle)
  • Improve forecast accuracy using time-based predictors
  • Evaluate model performance using MAE
  • Analyze forecast errors by hour of day

Dataset:¶

  • Source: CAISO (California Independent System Operator)
  • Resolution: Hourly demand data
  • Period: Jan 1, 2024 – Dec 31, 2025
  • Features: Timestamp, Demand (MW), etc

# Yesterday Naive Baseline Forecast

hourly["baseline_yesterday"] = hourly["Demand"].shift(24)

# Evaluation data
baseline_eval = hourly.loc[
    (hourly.index >= eval_start) &
    (hourly.index <= eval_end) &
    hourly["baseline_yesterday"].notna()
].copy()

# Standard columns used everywhere
baseline_eval["actual"] = baseline_eval["Demand"]
baseline_eval["forecast"] = baseline_eval["baseline_yesterday"]

# Absolute error
baseline_eval["abs_error"] = (
    baseline_eval["actual"] - baseline_eval["forecast"]
).abs()

# MAE
baseline_mae = baseline_eval["abs_error"].mean()
print(f"Yesterday Baseline MAE: {baseline_mae:.2f}")

# Plot
plt.figure(figsize=(14,5))
baseline_eval["actual"].plot(label="Actual Demand", color="black")
baseline_eval["forecast"].plot(label="Yesterday Baseline", color="orange", alpha=0.7)
plt.title("Yesterday Baseline vs Actual Demand")
plt.xlabel("Datetime")
plt.ylabel("Demand")
plt.legend()
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

# Hourly MAE
plt.figure(figsize=(10,4))
baseline_eval.groupby(baseline_eval.index.hour)["abs_error"].mean().plot()
plt.title("Yesterday Baseline Absolute Error by Hour")
plt.xlabel("Hour of Day")
plt.ylabel("MAE")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

# SARIMAX Forecast

# Training months
eval_months = hourly.loc[eval_start:eval_end].index.month.unique()

train_data = hourly.loc[
    (hourly.index < eval_start) &
    (hourly.index.month.isin(eval_months)),
    "Demand"
]

# Exogenous variables
train_exog = pd.DataFrame({
    "hour": train_data.index.hour,
    "dayofweek": train_data.index.dayofweek
}, index=train_data.index)

# Model
sarimax_model = SARIMAX(
    train_data,
    exog=train_exog,
    order=(1,0,1),
    seasonal_order=(1,1,1,24),
    trend='n',
    enforce_stationarity=False,
    enforce_invertibility=False
)

sarimax_result = sarimax_model.fit(disp=False)

# Forecast for evaluation window
eval_index = hourly.loc[eval_start:eval_end].index
steps = len(eval_index)

eval_exog = pd.DataFrame({
    "hour": eval_index.hour,
    "dayofweek": eval_index.dayofweek
}, index=eval_index)

forecast_obj = sarimax_result.get_forecast(
    steps=steps,
    exog=eval_exog
)

sarima_eval = pd.DataFrame({
    "actual": hourly.loc[eval_start:eval_end, "Demand"],
    "forecast": forecast_obj.predicted_mean.values
}, index=eval_index)

# Error
sarima_eval["abs_error"] = (
    sarima_eval["actual"] - sarima_eval["forecast"]
).abs()

sarima_mae = mean_absolute_error(
    sarima_eval["actual"],
    sarima_eval["forecast"]
)

print(f"SARIMAX MAE: {sarima_mae:.2f}")

# Plot
plt.figure(figsize=(14,5))
sarima_eval["actual"].plot(label="Actual Demand", color="black")
sarima_eval["forecast"].plot(label="SARIMAX Forecast", color="red")
plt.title("SARIMAX Forecast vs Actual Demand")
plt.xlabel("Datetime")
plt.ylabel("Demand")
plt.legend()
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

# Hourly MAE
plt.figure(figsize=(10,4))
sarima_eval.groupby(sarima_eval.index.hour)["abs_error"].mean().plot()
plt.title("SARIMAX Absolute Error by Hour")
plt.xlabel("Hour of Day")
plt.ylabel("MAE")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

# Prophet Forecast
eval_months = hourly.loc[eval_start:eval_end].index.month.unique()

train_df = hourly.loc[
    (hourly.index < eval_start) &
    (hourly.index.month.isin(eval_months)),
    "Demand"
].copy().reset_index()

print("Training months used:", eval_months)


train_df.columns = ["ds", "y"]
train_df["ds"] = pd.to_datetime(train_df["ds"])
train_df["y"] = train_df["y"].astype(float)

# Extra regressors
train_df["hour"] = train_df["ds"].dt.hour
train_df["dayofweek"] = train_df["ds"].dt.dayofweek
train_df["is_weekend"] = (train_df["dayofweek"] >= 5).astype(int)

# Model
prophet_model = Prophet(
    daily_seasonality=True,
    weekly_seasonality=True,
    yearly_seasonality=True,
    changepoint_prior_scale=.75,
    seasonality_prior_scale=10
)

prophet_model.add_regressor("hour")
prophet_model.add_regressor("dayofweek")
prophet_model.add_regressor("is_weekend")

prophet_model.fit(train_df)

# Forecast
eval_index = hourly.loc[eval_start:eval_end].index

future_df = pd.DataFrame({"ds": eval_index})
future_df["hour"] = future_df["ds"].dt.hour
future_df["dayofweek"] = future_df["ds"].dt.dayofweek
future_df["is_weekend"] = (future_df["dayofweek"] >= 5).astype(int)

forecast = prophet_model.predict(future_df)

# Force alignment by datetime
forecast = forecast.set_index("ds").reindex(eval_index)

prophet_eval = pd.DataFrame(index=eval_index)
prophet_eval["actual"] = hourly.loc[eval_index, "Demand"]
prophet_eval["forecast"] = forecast["yhat"]

# Error
prophet_eval["abs_error"] = (
    prophet_eval["actual"] - prophet_eval["forecast"]
).abs()

prophet_mae = prophet_eval["abs_error"].mean()

print(f"Prophet MAE: {prophet_mae:.2f}")

# Plot
plt.figure(figsize=(14,5))
prophet_eval["actual"].plot(label="Actual Demand", color="black")
prophet_eval["forecast"].plot(label="Prophet Forecast", color="blue")
plt.title("Prophet Forecast vs Actual Demand")
plt.xlabel("Datetime")
plt.ylabel("Demand")
plt.legend()
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

# Hourly MAE
plt.figure(figsize=(10,4))
prophet_eval.groupby(prophet_eval.index.hour)["abs_error"].mean().plot()
plt.title("Prophet Absolute Error by Hour")
plt.xlabel("Hour of Day")
plt.ylabel("MAE")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

Conclusion¶

In this project, I built and evaluated multiple approaches for forecasting hourly demand over a variable two-week period from January 1 2024 to December 31 2025. The objective was not simply to produce forecasts, but to understand how much performance improvement more sophisticated time-series methods could deliver relative to simple and highly interpretable baselines.

Modeling Strategy¶

I began by implementing two naïve benchmarks:

  • Yesterday baseline – assumes demand will match the same hour from the previous day.
  • Last-week baseline – assumes demand will match the same hour one week earlier.

These references are critical because they are inexpensive, transparent, and often surprisingly strong. Any advanced model must beat them to justify added complexity.

From there, I developed more advanced forecasting systems:

  • SARIMAX, incorporating autoregressive structure, daily seasonality, and calendar effects such as hour of day and day of week.
  • Prophet, leveraging built-in daily and weekly seasonal components with flexible changepoints.
  • A hybrid approach that blends model-based structure with recent observed behavior.

All data preparation, feature engineering, validation design, modeling, and diagnostics were completed independently.

Lessons Learned:¶

  1. Beating naive forecasts is hard. Simple methods set a very high bar.
  2. Recency matters. The most recent patterns can outweigh complex historical relationships.
  3. Model combinations are powerful. Blending approaches often yields more gain than tuning a single method.
